propositions.text: The rule of law requires all public power to have a legal source and limits set by statute, common law, or Constitution.
propositions.quote: The rule of law requires, among other things, that “the exercise of all public power must find its ultimate source in a legal rule”

propositions.text: The rule of law is a fundamental constitutional postulate requiring legal limits on public powers.
propositions.quote: The rule of law is a “fundamental postulate of our constitutional structure”: Roncarelli v. Duplessis

propositions.text: Unlimited power is not a legal power under the rule of law.
propositions.quote: An unlimited power is, definitionally, not a legal power.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the rule of law requires public power to have legal limits set by law or Constitution; unlimited power is not legal power.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns courts' constitutional role in preserving rule of law within the administrative state.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the constitutional role of the courts in preserving the rule of law within the administrative state.

propositions.text: Administrative decision-makers exercise delegated authority across government and policy areas, affecting Canadians' daily lives.
propositions.quote: Administrative decision-makers exercise delegated authority at every level of government and in every area of policy.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns courts' constitutional role in preserving rule of law over administrative decision-makers exercising delegated authority.

propositions.text: Since Crevier, judicial review of administrative decision-makers is constitutionally guaranteed by ss. 96-101 of Constitution Act, 1867.
propositions.quote: Since at least this Court’s decision in Crevier v. Attorney General of Quebec... some minimum of judicial review... is guaranteed by the Constitution.

propositions.text: Superior courts are guardians of rule of law and have supervisory jurisdiction over executive through judicial review.
propositions.quote: The judicature provisions... enshrine the superior courts as guardians of the rule of law and constitutionally guarantee... supervisory jurisdiction over the executive through judicial review.

propositions.text: Judicial review ensures statutory powers are not exceeded and is constitutionally guaranteed; legislatures cannot fully shield administrative decisions from review.
propositions.quote: Judicial review is intimately connected with the preservation of the rule of law... legislatures cannot shield administrative decision making from curial scrutiny entirely.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains judicial review is constitutionally guaranteed to supervise administrative powers and cannot be fully shielded by legislatures.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch argues constitutional judicial review guarantees core minimum legality review of all administrative decisions, immune to ordinary legislation.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Democracy Watch, submits that the constitutional guarantee of judicial review must entail a core constitutional minimum of legality review of all aspects of an administrative decision.

propositions.text: Attorney General of Canada argues constitutional minimum judicial review is narrower, only jurisdictional review guaranteed; legislatures may oust review on fact or law not touching jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The respondent, the Attorney General of Canada, submits that the core constitutional minimum of judicial review is narrower... only jurisdictional review is constitutionally guaranteed.

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch argues for broad constitutional judicial review; Canada argues only jurisdictional review is guaranteed constitutionally.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal held judicial review on fact and law is constitutionally guaranteed; legislative ousters on these grounds are unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal has held that judicial review on questions of fact and law is constitutionally guaranteed... legislative efforts to oust review... are unconstitutional.

propositions.text: This Court has not yet explicitly defined constitutional guarantee of judicial review or addressed constitutionality of legislative limits on review.
propositions.quote: However, this Court has not yet explicitly defined the constitutional guarantee of judicial review, nor directly addressed the constitutionality of legislative mechanisms that purport to limit judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal held broad constitutional judicial review; this Court has not yet defined the constitutional guarantee or addressed legislative limits.

propositions.text: The issue is whether s. 66 of COIA validly bars judicial review on questions of fact and law or is inoperative as unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: To decide Democracy Watch’s appeal, we must determine if the partial privative clause in s. 66 of the Conflict of Interest Act... is a valid bar to judicial review on questions of fact and law...

paragraphs.summary: The Court frames the issue as whether s. 66 of COIA validly bars judicial review on fact and law questions or is unconstitutional.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and matter remanded; courts exclusively review legality of delegated power under Constitution ss. 96-101.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and remand the matter to the Federal Court of Appeal. The authority to review the legality... is the exclusive preserve of the courts...

propositions.text: Legal powers are bounded; delegated authority has limits and must be used consistent with its purpose.
propositions.quote: All delegated power has limits, and no authority may be used in a manner inconsistent with the purpose for which it is granted.

paragraphs.summary: The Court would allow the appeal, remand, and affirms courts' exclusive constitutional role to review legality of delegated powers with bounded limits.

propositions.text: Legality review of all administrative decisions is constitutionally guaranteed; s. 66 COIA infringing this is of no force and effect.
propositions.quote: The availability of this “legality review” is constitutionally guaranteed... Section 66 of the COIA infringes this guarantee... it is of no force and effect.

propositions.text: Constitution guarantees legality review of all aspects of administrative decisions; courts have supervisory jurisdiction over public authority.
propositions.quote: Every exercise of public authority is subject to the courts’ supervisory jurisdiction... The availability of this “legality review” is constitutionally guaranteed.

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds constitutionally guaranteed legality review applies to all administrative decisions; s. 66 COIA is invalid to the extent it bars review.

propositions.text: In May 2021, Ethics Commissioner reported PM Trudeau did not contravene COIA in WE Charity funding decisions after investigation.
propositions.quote: On May 14, 2021, the Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner released a report concluding that then Prime Minister Justin Trudeau had not contravened the COIA...

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the Ethics Commissioner found PM Trudeau did not breach COIA in WE Charity funding decisions after investigation.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch applied for judicial review alleging errors of fact and law in Commissioner's COIA interpretation and application.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch applied to the Federal Court of Appeal for judicial review of the Commissioner’s decision. Democracy Watch alleged that the Commissioner made errors of fact and law...

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch applied for judicial review alleging errors of fact and law in the Commissioner's COIA decision.

propositions.text: Attorney General of Canada moved to strike application, arguing Democracy Watch lacked standing and s. 66 COIA bars judicial review on fact and law.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada brought a motion to strike Democracy Watch’s application for judicial review. Canada argued that Democracy Watch lacked standing and that its application was barred by s. 66 of the COIA...

paragraphs.summary: Canada moved to strike Democracy Watch's application, arguing lack of standing and s. 66 COIA bars judicial review on fact and law.

propositions.text: Motion judge found Democracy Watch had public interest standing but deferred s. 66 bar question to full panel and split proceedings into two stages.
propositions.quote: The motion judge determined that Democracy Watch had public interest standing... he deferred to a full panel the question of whether s. 66 was a bar... ordered the proceedings to be split into two stages.

paragraphs.summary: The motion judge found Democracy Watch had standing but deferred s. 66 issue to full panel and split proceedings into two stages.

propositions.text: Full Federal Court of Appeal panel dismissed Democracy Watch's application, citing adequate alternative political remedies.
propositions.quote: In its decision following the Stage 1 hearing, the full panel of the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed Democracy Watch’s application. It concluded that there were adequate alternative political remedies...

propositions.text: Chief Justice de Montigny would have upheld s. 66 COIA as valid bar to judicial review; majority disagreed, relying on prior binding decisions.
propositions.quote: Chief Justice de Montigny would have also held that s. 66 of the COIA was valid... His majority colleagues disagreed... dismissed the application on the sole basis of adequate alternative remedies.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal panel dismissed application citing alternative remedies; Chief Justice would uphold s. 66 bar, majority disagreed.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch appeals to set aside Federal Court of Appeal order and proceed to Stage 2; appeal limited to two grounds.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch asks this Court to set aside the order of the Federal Court of Appeal and remand the application to proceed to Stage 2.

propositions.text: Grounds of appeal: 1) Did Federal Court err in declining judicial review due to adequate alternative remedy? 2) Can s. 66 COIA bar judicial review on fact and law?
propositions.quote: It bears emphasis that this appeal does not concern the merits... beyond the following two grounds of appeal...

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch appeals to set aside dismissal and proceed; grounds are adequacy of alternative remedy and constitutionality of s. 66 COIA bar.

propositions.text: The Court will address each ground of appeal in turn.
propositions.quote: I address each ground of appeal in turn.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it will address each ground of appeal in turn.

propositions.text: There is no adequate alternative to judicial review of Commissioner's decision; political process cannot directly challenge legality.
propositions.quote: there is no adequate alternative to judicial review of the Commissioner’s decision... no mechanism other than judicial review whereby the legality... may be challenged directly.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal erred in dismissing application based on adequate alternative remedy.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal erred in dismissing Democracy Watch’s application on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds no adequate alternative to judicial review exists and Federal Court of Appeal erred in dismissing application on that basis.

propositions.text: Persons with standing have constitutional right to apply for judicial review; courts must consider appropriateness of review.
propositions.quote: persons with standing to challenge administrative decisions have a right, as a matter of constitutional principle, to apply for judicial review

propositions.text: Granting relief on judicial review is discretionary; courts need not engage merits if basis to decline relief exists.
propositions.quote: the decision to grant relief on an application for judicial review is discretionary; where there is a basis to decline relief, a court need not engage with the merits

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites precedent that persons with standing have right to apply for judicial review, but relief is discretionary and may be declined.

propositions.text: Adequate alternative remedy must provide oversight of legality of administrative action; otherwise judicial review should not be deferred.
propositions.quote: An alternative remedy is adequate only if it provides an alternative “channel for oversight of the legality . . . of administrative action”

propositions.text: Availability of adequate alternative remedy is a discretionary basis to refuse judicial review.
propositions.quote: Among the discretionary bases for refusing judicial review is the availability of an adequate alternative remedy

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains adequate alternative remedy must provide legality oversight; availability of such remedy is discretionary basis to refuse judicial review.

propositions.text: Alternative remedy need not be identical to judicial review but must be adequate in all circumstances to address applicant's concern.
propositions.quote: For an alternative remedy to be adequate, its process and the remedies it offers need not be identical to those available on judicial review.

propositions.text: Courts must consider suitability and appropriateness of judicial review, including forum advantages, accessibility, and remedies available.
propositions.quote: A court must “consider not only the available alternative, but also the suitability and appropriateness of judicial review in the circumstances”

paragraphs.summary: The Court states alternative remedies need not be identical but must be adequate; courts consider suitability, accessibility, and remedies in deciding review appropriateness.

propositions.text: Where alternative forum adequately reviews legality and orders remedy, judicial review is unnecessary and courts may decline review.
propositions.quote: where a statutory regime makes available an alternative forum in which the legality of an impugned administrative decision may be adequately reviewed... judicial review is unnecessary

paragraphs.summary: The Court states if an alternative forum adequately reviews legality and remedies, judicial review is unnecessary and may be declined.

propositions.text: Discretionary decisions to decline judicial review are reviewable for legal or palpable errors, irrelevant or missing factors, or wrong principles.
propositions.quote: An exercise of discretion to decline judicial review will be vulnerable to appellate review if it was based on an error of law or a palpable and overriding error of fact, on consideration of irrelevant factors, on a failure to consider relevant factors, or on a “wrong principle”: Yatar, at para. 41

propositions.text: Discretionary decisions not to consider judicial review merits are owed deference but not immune from appellate oversight.
propositions.quote: The discretionary decision of a court not to consider an application for judicial review on its merits is not immune from appellate oversight, though it is owed deference: Yatar, at para. 41; Strickland, at para. 39; Canadian Pacific Ltd. v. Matsqui Indian Band, [1995] 1 S.C.R. 3, at para. 39.

paragraphs.summary: The court states discretionary decisions declining judicial review are reviewable for errors of law, fact, or principle, citing prior authorities.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal found COIA provides political oversight of Commissioner as adequate alternative to judicial review.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal held that the COIA provided for political oversight of the Commissioner’s activities and that this oversight was an adequate alternative to judicial supervision.

propositions.text: COIA intended to provide dual parliamentary and judicial oversight of Commissioner.
propositions.quote: It held that the COIA was intended to provide for “dual parliamentary and judicial oversight”: para. 92.

propositions.text: Commissioner is independent Officer of Parliament acting under House of Commons direction enforcing code to members.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner “is an independent Officer of Parliament, and the position he occupies is firmly within the legislative branch of government . . . he acts under the direction of the House of Commons when enforcing the code to its members”: para. 80.

propositions.text: Commissioner must submit annual reports to Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner is required to submit annual reports on the administration of the COIA to the Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics.

propositions.text: Reporting mechanism provides political oversight adequate alternative to judicial review.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal held that this reporting mechanism provided an avenue for political oversight that was an adequate alternative to judicial review: paras. 83 and 88.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal found COIA's political oversight and reporting mechanisms provide an adequate alternative to judicial review.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal relied on Auditor General case to support political oversight as alternative to judicial review.
propositions.quote: In reaching its conclusion, the Federal Court of Appeal relied on this Court’s decision in Canada (Auditor General) v. Canada (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 49.

propositions.text: Auditor General sought judicial review of Governor in Council’s refusal to provide information for audit.
propositions.quote: In that case, the Auditor General sought judicial review of the Governor in Council’s decision not to order certain information be made available to him for the purposes of performing an audit.

propositions.text: Court declined to review Governor in Council’s decision because Auditor General had political recourse via Parliament.
propositions.quote: This Court declined to review the decision of the Governor in Council.

propositions.text: Auditor General reported annually to House of Commons on information access under Auditor General Act.
propositions.quote: Under s. 7(1) of the Auditor General Act, S.C. 1976-77, c. 34, as then in force, the Auditor General reported annually to the House of Commons “on whether, in carrying on the work of his office, he received all the information . . . required”: Auditor General, at p. 98.

propositions.text: Parliament is final arbiter of disputes over Auditor General’s access to information, providing political remedy.
propositions.quote: Parliament “designated itself as final arbiter of any disputes over the Auditor General’s access to information”: p. 100.

propositions.text: Auditor General’s report to House of Commons brings government refusal to provide information to public attention.
propositions.quote: A report by the Auditor General to the House of Commons that the government of the day has refused to provide information brings the matter to public attention. (Auditor General, at p. 104)

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal relied on Auditor General case where political oversight via Parliament was adequate alternative to judicial review.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal held COIA reporting mechanism is similarly an adequate political remedy.
propositions.quote: According to the Federal Court of Appeal, “the same can be said of the reporting mechanism found in the COIA”: para. 88.

propositions.text: Courts should exercise judicial restraint respecting separation of powers and limits in section 66 of COIA.
propositions.quote: the courts should “exercise judicial restraint and adhere to the limits prescribed by section 66 of the COIA”: paras. 89 and 92.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal found COIA reporting is an adequate political remedy and courts should exercise judicial restraint under section 66.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch argues court below misapplied adequate alternative remedy doctrine and misunderstood COIA scheme.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch submits that the court below misapplied the doctrine of adequate alternative remedy, misunderstood the statutory scheme of the COIA, and relied on distinguishable authorities to reach its conclusion.

propositions.text: Canada argues no error below and political mechanisms under COIA adequately address issues raised by Democracy Watch.
propositions.quote: Canada submits that the court below made no error, and that the questions of fact and law raised by Democracy Watch can be adequately addressed by political mechanisms provided under the COIA.

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch argues the court erred on adequate alternative remedy; Canada defends the court's decision and political mechanisms under COIA.

propositions.text: I agree with Democracy Watch that the court below erred.
propositions.quote: I agree with Democracy Watch.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Democracy Watch's position.

propositions.text: Commissioner administers COIA and MP Code under Parliament of Canada Act.
propositions.quote: Under the COIA and the Parliament of Canada Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-1 (“PCA”), the Commissioner administers both the COIA and the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, App. I, Conflict of Interest and Ethics Code for Members of the House of Commons (April 2026) (“MP Code”).

propositions.text: PCA section 86(3) states Commissioner acts under House of Commons general direction for MP Code.
propositions.quote: In this latter capacity, the PCA is explicit that the Commissioner acts under the “general direction” of the House of Commons: s. 86(3).

propositions.text: PCA section 86(4) states Commissioner does not act under House direction when administering COIA for ministers.
propositions.quote: But the PCA is equally clear that the Commissioner does not act under the direction of the House of Commons where, as here, he is administering the COIA with respect to “ministers of the Crown, ministers of state or parliamentary secretaries acting in their capacity as ministers of the Crown, ministers of state or parliamentary secretaries”: s. 86(4).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Commissioner administers COIA and MP Code, acting under House direction only for MP Code, not for COIA regarding ministers.

propositions.text: Canada agrees parliamentary privilege applies only to MP Code administration, not COIA for public office holders.
propositions.quote: Canada agrees that parliamentary privilege applies only to the Commissioner’s work in administering the MP Code, and not when he administers the COIA with respect to public office holders, a separate responsibility: R.F., at para. 59.

propositions.text: Canada endorses Federal Court of Appeal’s analysis respecting Parliament’s institutional design and separation of powers.
propositions.quote: But Canada endorses the Federal Court of Appeal’s analysis on the basis that it evinces the appropriate respect for Parliament’s institutional design choices and the separation of powers.

paragraphs.summary: Canada agrees parliamentary privilege applies only to MP Code, endorses Federal Court of Appeal's respect for Parliament's design and separation of powers.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal failed to analyze appropriateness and suitability of judicial review, missing Strickland factors.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal’s reasons do not demonstrate the required analysis of the appropriateness and suitability of judicial review in the circumstances: Strickland, at para. 43.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal must ensure COIA provides adequate alternative forum for legality review of Commissioner’s decision.
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal was required to satisfy itself that the COIA provided an alternative forum in which the legality of the Commissioner’s decision could be adequately reviewed: Yatar, at para. 61.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Federal Court of Appeal failed to analyze judicial review suitability and adequacy of alternative forum under COIA.

propositions.text: Auditor General case involved officer of Parliament seeking judicial review, unlike private party here.
propositions.quote: Auditor General concerned an application to the courts made by an officer of Parliament against a decision of the Governor in Council.

propositions.text: Auditor General could seek remedy from Parliament under statute, unlike Democracy Watch here.
propositions.quote: Under his enabling statute, the Auditor General could go before Parliament and seek, in effect, the same remedy he sought from the courts.

propositions.text: Auditor General had statutory duty to report to House of Commons on information access.
propositions.quote: Under s. 7(1) he was empowered, and indeed required, to report to the House of Commons on whether he was receiving the information he needed to fulfill his mandate: p. 98.

propositions.text: Parliament could require Governor in Council to provide information to Auditor General exercising sovereign authority.
propositions.quote: Parliament could then require that the Governor in Council make available to the Auditor General that information which he needed to fulfill his mandate, exercising its sovereign authority over the executive.

propositions.text: Court declined to usurp Parliament’s role as final arbiter in Auditor General case.
propositions.quote: Because this avenue for redress was available to him, the Court rightly declined to usurp the arbitral role Parliament had assigned itself: p. 100.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes Auditor General case as involving an officer with parliamentary remedy, unlike Democracy Watch's private party challenge.

propositions.text: Commissioner’s annual report to Parliament under COIA is of little assistance to Democracy Watch.
propositions.quote: While the Commissioner has a facially similar reporting obligation under s. 90(1)(b) of the PCA, it is hard to see how such an annual report by the Commissioner to Parliament is of any assistance to Democracy Watch.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch cannot ask Parliament or others to review Commissioner’s report under COIA.
propositions.quote: Here Democracy Watch has no recourse under the COIA to ask Parliament, or anyone other than the courts, to review the Commissioner’s report.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Commissioner’s report to Parliament under COIA does not help Democracy Watch, which lacks recourse except courts.

propositions.text: COIA section 47 states Commissioner’s conclusions are final and may not be altered by anyone.
propositions.quote: Indeed, the COIA is explicit that the Commissioner’s conclusions are final and “may not be altered by anyone”: s. 47.

propositions.text: Even if Democracy Watch could bring concerns to Parliament, no political remedy could alter Commissioner’s report.
propositions.quote: Even if Democracy Watch could bring its concerns before Parliament, it is hard to see what political remedy Democracy Watch could expect, since the report itself, if valid, cannot be altered.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes COIA makes Commissioner’s conclusions final and unalterable, limiting political remedies for Democracy Watch.

propositions.text: Auditor General case holdings are limited to its facts and unique statute role.
propositions.quote: Chief Justice Dickson’s concluding remarks in Auditor General, where he took pains to limit his holdings to the facts of that case: . . . the holdings in this case should be viewed as limited to the interpretation of a unique statute as informed by the particular role played by the Auditor General.

propositions.text: Courts should not readily decline remedies for rights recognized by Canadian law.
propositions.quote: The above analysis shall not be taken to detract from the fundamental principle that the courts should not readily decline to grant remedies for rights recognized by the laws of Canada.

propositions.text: Auditor General is distinguishable and not a broad precedent on adequacy of political remedies.
propositions.quote: Auditor General is not only clearly distinguishable, it was never intended to stand for a broader proposition with respect to the adequacy of political remedies.

propositions.text: Questions of legality remain reviewable by courts despite political remedies.
propositions.quote: the general principle remains that questions of legality are reviewable by the courts.

paragraphs.summary: The court limits Auditor General case to its facts, emphasizing courts must not decline remedies and legality questions remain reviewable.

propositions.text: COIA provides no alternative forum for interested parties to seek judicial review of Commissioner’s report legality.
propositions.quote: There is nothing in the COIA that provides interested parties like Democracy Watch with an alternative forum in which to seek the remedy available on judicial review: consideration of the legality of the Commissioner’s report.

propositions.text: COIA section 47 states Commissioner’s conclusions cannot be changed by anyone unless quashed by court.
propositions.quote: While s. 47 of the COIA makes clear that the report is not determinative of enforcement measures that will be taken on the basis of the Commissioner’s conclusions, it provides explicitly that these conclusions cannot be changed by anyone.

propositions.text: Commissioner’s conclusions cannot be altered unless judicial review quashes the decision.
propositions.quote: Unless the Commissioner’s decision is quashed following judicial review, his conclusions cannot be altered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds COIA offers no alternative forum for legality review and Commissioner’s conclusions are final unless quashed by court.

propositions.text: Parliament retains meaningful role supervising Commissioner’s activities and enforcement of recommendations.
propositions.quote: Parliament retains a meaningful role in supervising the conduct of the Commissioner’s activities, and in choosing whether and how to give effect to his recommendations.

propositions.text: Courts must supervise and remedy unlawful exercise of Commissioner’s statutory powers exceeding limits.
propositions.quote: Where it is alleged that the Commissioner has exercised his statutory powers in a manner that exceeds their limits, the rule of law requires that the courts be able to exercise their supervisory jurisdiction to remedy any unlawful exercise of legal authority.

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes Parliament’s supervisory role but courts must remedy unlawful excesses of Commissioner’s statutory powers.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal erred in concluding political oversight is adequate alternative to judicial review.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal erred in concluding that political oversight of the Commissioner’s activities, generally, was an adequate alternative to judicial review of his report.

propositions.text: This error of law requires appellate intervention as no adequate alternative remedy exists to justify discretion not to consider judicial review.
propositions.quote: This is an error of law that requires appellate intervention. There is no adequate alternative remedy that could justify the Federal Court of Appeal’s exercise of discretion not to consider Democracy Watch’s application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Federal Court of Appeal erred legally, requiring intervention as no adequate alternative remedy exists.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal did not consider applicability and validity of COIA section 66 due to adequate alternative remedy conclusion.
propositions.quote: Because it concluded that there was an adequate alternative remedy, the majority of the Federal Court of Appeal did not go on to consider in any detail the question the motion judge had referred to the panel: the applicability and validity of s. 66 of the COIA.

propositions.text: Canada submits that even if adequate alternative remedy conclusion was error, dismissal was still correct due to section 66 ousting judicial review.
propositions.quote: Canada submits that, even if the Federal Court of Appeal erred in concluding there was an adequate alternative remedy, it was still right to dismiss the application. Canada endorses de Montigny C.J.’s minority opinion, which concluded that s. 66 of the COIA validly ousts judicial review on questions of fact and law.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch submits section 66 cannot bar constitutionally guaranteed legality review on fact and law questions.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch submits that legality review on questions of fact and law is constitutionally guaranteed, and as such s. 66 cannot bar judicial review of the Commissioner’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal did not consider COIA section 66; Canada argues it bars judicial review, Democracy Watch argues it cannot.

propositions.text: I agree with Democracy Watch that section 66 cannot bar judicial review of Commissioner’s decision.
propositions.quote: I agree with Democracy Watch.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Democracy Watch that section 66 cannot bar judicial review.

propositions.text: Sections 96 to 101 of Constitution Act, 1867 guarantee superior courts’ inherent jurisdiction and protect core aspects.
propositions.quote: The judicature provisions in ss. 96 to 101 of the Constitution Act, 1867 guarantee the existence of superior courts of inherent jurisdiction and protect the core, essential aspects of that jurisdiction: see Reference re Code of Civil Procedure (Que.), art. 35, 2021 SCC 27, [2021] 2 S.C.R. 291 (“CCP Reference”), at para. 63; Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court, at para. 124; MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 725, at paras. 36-37; Toronto (City) v. Ontario (Attorney General), 2021 SCC 34, [2021] 2 S.C.R. 845, at para. 55; Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2014 SCC 59, [2014] 3 S.C.R. 31, at paras. 28-29 and 38-39; U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 1048, at p. 1090.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Constitution Act sections 96-101 guarantee superior courts’ inherent jurisdiction and protect core aspects.

propositions.text: Core constitutional jurisdiction of superior courts includes legality review, enforcement, process control, and residual original jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The core constitutional jurisdiction of the superior courts protected under ss. 96 to 101 encompasses “the powers and jurisdiction essential to [the superior courts’] role as the cornerstone of the unitary justice system and the primary guardians of the rule of law”: CCP Reference, at para. 63. The “review of the legality and constitutional validity of laws, enforcement of its orders, control over its own process, and its residual jurisdiction as a court of original general jurisdiction” are all included within this constitutionally protected core of the courts’ jurisdiction: para. 68.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains superior courts’ core constitutional jurisdiction includes legality review and enforcement as guardians of the rule of law.

propositions.text: Judicial review of public powers is essential to courts' constitutional function and rule of law protection.
propositions.quote: The supervision of the administrative state through judicial review of the exercise of public powers is one of these essential aspects of the courts’ constitutional function

propositions.text: Legislative attempts to limit superior courts' core jurisdiction are ultra vires under Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 96-101.
propositions.quote: Legislative efforts to limit the core jurisdiction of the superior courts are ultra vires: they trench on the powers assigned exclusively to the courts by ss. 96 to 101 of the Constitution Act, 1867.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states judicial review is essential to courts' constitutional role and legislative limits on superior courts' jurisdiction are ultra vires.

propositions.text: Privative clauses cannot shield administrative decision-makers from judicial review on jurisdiction questions.
propositions.quote: a privative clause cannot shield an administrative decision-maker from judicial review on questions of jurisdiction

propositions.text: Privative clauses may oust judicial review on questions of law and other non-jurisdictional issues if properly framed.
propositions.quote: privative clauses may, when properly framed, effectively oust judicial review on questions of law and, indeed, on other issues not touching jurisdiction

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains Crevier held privative clauses cannot shield jurisdictional review but may oust review on law and other issues.

propositions.text: Canada argues Crevier means judicial review on fact and law can be barred by partial privative clauses.
propositions.quote: Canada says this language from Crevier means that judicial review on questions of fact and law fall outside the scope of the constitutional guarantee, and can be barred by a partial privative clause

propositions.text: Democracy Watch argues Crevier's jurisdictional review includes legality review on all decision aspects, including fact and law.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch disagrees. It submits that Crevier must be read in its historical context, and that the jurisdictional review which Crevier identified as constitutionally guaranteed encompasses legality review on all aspects of an administrative decision, including questions of fact and law.

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues Crevier allows barring review on fact and law; Democracy Watch says jurisdictional review includes all legality review.

propositions.text: Crevier fits the evolution from correctness to reasonableness review and shows constitutional minimum of judicial review includes legality review of all administrative decisions.
propositions.quote: Crevier is not an outlier: it fits neatly into the long arc of Canadian administrative law away from a strict conception of judicial review as correctness review towards deference and the presumption of reasonableness review set out in Vavilov

propositions.text: Courts' power to review public power exercises to guard against unlawful government action is constitutionally guaranteed.
propositions.quote: Our jurisprudence has long recognized that the power of the courts to review exercises of public power, so as to guard against unlawful government action in any form, is constitutionally guaranteed

propositions.text: Efforts to shield any part of an administrative decision from legality review are unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: Efforts to shield any aspect of an administrative decision from legality review are therefore unconstitutional

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds Crevier aligns with evolving law and guarantees constitutional judicial review of legality on all administrative decisions.

propositions.text: CUPE marks the shift from old to modern Canadian administrative law.
propositions.quote: This Court’s decision in Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (“CUPE”), is widely recognized as the demarcation between the ancien régime of Canadian administrative law and the modern era

propositions.text: Before CUPE, courts followed the jurisdictional error model from Anisminic endorsed by this Court.
propositions.quote: Prior to CUPE, Canadian courts largely followed the “jurisdictional error” model of administrative review encapsulated in the House of Lords’ decision in Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission, [1969] 2 A.C. 147, which was endorsed by this Court

propositions.text: Anisminic was the canonical example of the orthodox approach to judicial review influenced by Dicey's court-centric rule of law view.
propositions.quote: Anisminic was the “canonical example” of the orthodox approach to judicial review, which germinated in the long shadow of Professor A. V. Dicey’s court-centric view of the rule of law

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains CUPE marks the shift from Anisminic's jurisdictional error model influenced by Dicey's rule of law view.

propositions.text: Jurisdictional error model treated decisions within statutory scope as unreviewable and arbitrary, opposing rule of law.
propositions.quote: The jurisdictional error model regarded administrative decisions taken within the scope of a body’s statutory jurisdiction as unreviewable; these decisions were, in the Diceyan imagination, not “law” at all, but simply exercises of arbitrary discretion

propositions.text: Courts guarded jurisdiction boundaries; errors in law, fact, or natural justice breaches made decisions null and reviewable de novo.
propositions.quote: where an administrative body exceeded its legislative authority — by, for instance, erring in law, making an unreasonable finding of fact, or breaching the laws of natural justice — its decision was a nullity and the courts would adjudicate the question de novo

propositions.text: Privative clauses cannot shield jurisdictional errors from review; limits of tribunal powers cannot be bypassed by privative clauses.
propositions.quote: A jurisdictional error also entitled the courts to ignore a privative clause, no matter how clearly or expansively worded

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the jurisdictional error model treating decisions within jurisdiction as unreviewable but errors as nullities not shielded by privative clauses.

propositions.text: CUPE recognized difficulty in defining jurisdictional questions and allowed privative clauses to shield errors unless patently unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Justice Dickson ... observed that “what is and is not jurisdictional is often very difficult to determine” ... The only question for the reviewing court was whether ... the board had reached a conclusion “so patently unreasonable” as to result in a loss of jurisdiction

paragraphs.summary: CUPE held jurisdictional questions are hard to define and privative clauses protect decisions unless patently unreasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is a fundamental limit on delegated power; administrative bodies have jurisdiction to err but not to be unreasonable.
propositions.quote: an administrative body “has the necessary jurisdiction to make a mistake, and even a serious one, but not to be unreasonable”

paragraphs.summary: The Court states reasonableness limits administrative power; bodies may err but not act unreasonably.

propositions.text: CUPE did not displace that unreasonableness exceeds jurisdiction; it set jurisprudence towards reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: Nothing in CUPE displaced the principle that administrative decision-makers lacked the jurisdiction to act unreasonably

paragraphs.summary: CUPE confirmed unreasonableness exceeds jurisdiction and led jurisprudence towards reasonableness review.

propositions.text: Post-CUPE, reasonable decisions are valid even if incorrect; correctness review scope declined to narrow categories after Vavilov.
propositions.quote: Since CUPE, the dominant approach has been to treat reasonable decisions as valid even where they are “incorrect” ... After Vavilov, only a few narrow categories of issues attract correctness review

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains reasonableness review predominates post-CUPE, with correctness review limited after Vavilov.

propositions.text: Patently unreasonable factual and legal findings exceed jurisdiction and remain jurisdictional errors after CUPE.
propositions.quote: patently unreasonable exercises of delegated power, including on questions of both fact and law, were still jurisdictional errors after CUPE

propositions.text: More questions are reviewed on reasonableness standard rather than correctness over time.
propositions.quote: more and more questions came to be reviewed on that standard, rather than on a standard of correctness

paragraphs.summary: Patently unreasonable decisions remain jurisdictional errors, but more questions are reviewed on reasonableness than correctness.

propositions.text: Southam introduced reasonableness simpliciter as an intermediary standard before Dunsmuir.
propositions.quote: In Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., ... the Court introduced an intermediary standard of “reasonableness simpliciter”

paragraphs.summary: Southam introduced reasonableness simpliciter as an intermediate standard before Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: Distinction between unreasonable and patently unreasonable decisions was inconsistent and flawed.
propositions.quote: The distinction between an unreasonable decision and a patently unreasonable decision proved difficult to ascertain on any consistent or principled basis

propositions.text: Dunsmuir recognized rationality as binary: a decision is either rational or not.
propositions.quote: The Dunsmuir Court recognized that rationality was a binary consideration; a decision either was rational or it was not

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes the distinction between unreasonable and patently unreasonable decisions was flawed; Dunsmuir treats rationality as binary.

propositions.text: Dunsmuir endorsed that irrational decisions invalidate administrative decisions as beyond power.
propositions.quote: an irrational decision is an invalid decision because it is not the kind of decision an administrative decision-maker is empowered to make

paragraphs.summary: Dunsmuir held irrational decisions are invalid as beyond administrative power.

propositions.text: Irrationality reflects lack of jurisdiction; legal powers have essential limits including rationality.
propositions.quote: An irrational decision is an invalid decision because it is not the kind of decision an administrative decision-maker is empowered to make. Legal powers are given for purposes, and subject to limits; rationality is among the most essential of those limits.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states irrational decisions exceed jurisdiction as legal powers have essential limits including rationality.

propositions.text: Dunsmuir narrowed jurisdiction questions to correctness review but rejected old jurisdiction/preliminary question doctrine.
propositions.quote: The Dunsmuir Court held that “true” questions of jurisdiction attracted correctness review, but noted that it did not “wish nor intend to return to the jurisdiction/preliminary question doctrine

propositions.text: Courts questioned utility of true jurisdiction questions category due to uncertainty.
propositions.quote: the Court increasingly questioned its utility

paragraphs.summary: Dunsmuir narrowed jurisdiction questions to correctness review but courts questioned the category's utility due to uncertainty.

propositions.text: Vavilov made reasonableness the presumptive standard, abolishing true jurisdiction questions category.
propositions.quote: Vavilov ... recognized that reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review ... the Court concluded that the category of “true questions of jurisdiction” was no longer useful and did away with it

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov established reasonableness as presumptive standard and abolished true jurisdiction questions category.

propositions.text: Vavilov balanced courts' duty to police legality with respect for legislative intent in reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: reasonableness review balances the constitutional duty of the courts to police the boundaries of legality with the constitutional imperative to respect legislative intent

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov balanced courts' duty to police legality with respect for legislative intent in reasonableness review.

propositions.text: Privative clauses evolved with jurisdictional review, evidencing legislative intent to delegate questions to administrative bodies.
propositions.quote: Privative clauses were key to the CUPE-era move from Anisminic-style interventionism to deferential review. Privative clauses were incontrovertible evidence of legislative intent to leave certain questions with the legislature’s delegate

paragraphs.summary: Privative clauses evolved as evidence of legislative intent to delegate questions to administrative bodies.

propositions.text: Privative clauses became less relevant as deferential review grew; serious errors like unreasonableness cannot be shielded by privative clauses.
propositions.quote: a sufficiently serious error — quintessentially, an unreasonable exercise of delegated power — could not be shielded from review by any privative clause

paragraphs.summary: Privative clauses lost relevance with deferential review; serious errors like unreasonableness remain reviewable despite privative clauses.

propositions.text: Post-CUPE, privative clauses signal legislative intent favoring reasonableness review over correctness review.
propositions.quote: In the post-CUPE era, the presence of a privative clause became a signal of legislative intent that militated in favour of reasonableness review over correctness review

propositions.text: Dunsmuir states courts' power to review administrative decisions is constitutionally protected and cannot be removed by legislature.
propositions.quote: The rule of law requires that the constitutional role of superior courts be preserved and, as indicated above, neither Parliament nor any legislature can completely remove the courts’ power to review the actions and decisions of administrative bodies. This power is constitutionally protected.

propositions.text: Judicial review ensures privative clauses are read in context and administrative bodies do not exceed jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Judicial review is necessary to ensure that the privative clause is read in its appropriate statutory context and that administrative bodies do not exceed their jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains post-CUPE privative clauses favor reasonableness review; Dunsmuir confirms courts' review power is constitutionally protected and necessary.

propositions.text: By Vavilov, privative clauses no longer independently determine standard of review; reasonableness review is presumed.
propositions.quote: By the time Vavilov overtook Dunsmuir, privative clauses no longer served an independent or additional function in identifying the standard of review

propositions.text: Legislative intent guides judicial review scope; empowering statute scheme informs discretion and legal constraints on decision-makers.
propositions.quote: legislative intent remains the “polar star” of judicial review, as it informs the scope of the grant of power to the legislature’s delegate

propositions.text: Privative clauses evolved from ignored 'paper tigers' to integrated statutory scheme parts irrelevant to courts' supervisory jurisdiction scope.
propositions.quote: Privative clauses have gone from the paper tigers of the Anisminic era, ignored almost entirely, to an integrated part of the statutory scheme, irrelevant to the scope of the courts’ supervisory jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Vavilov presumes reasonableness review regardless of privative clauses, which now integrate into statutory schemes but don't affect courts' supervisory jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Crevier involved a provincial tribunal with powers violating s. 96 of Constitution Act, 1867.
propositions.quote: Crevier concerned a provincial tribunal with powers so broad they contravened the prohibition in s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867

propositions.text: Crevier's dictum affirms constitutional guarantee of judicial review on jurisdictional questions as legality review.
propositions.quote: Crevier’s statement that judicial review on jurisdictional questions is constitutionally protected must be understood to mean that the courts’ ability to conduct legality review is constitutionally guaranteed.

propositions.text: Crevier reflected post-CUPE shift from strict correctness to deferential review respecting legislative intent; privative clauses can shield non-jurisdictional questions from review.
propositions.quote: Crevier observed that questions of law and other questions not touching jurisdiction could be shielded from judicial review by a privative clause

paragraphs.summary: Crevier involved unconstitutional tribunal powers but affirmed constitutional guarantee of legality review; it reflected post-CUPE deferential review and privative clause limits.

propositions.text: Judicial review in Anisminic era meant correctness review substituting court's view for tribunal's.
propositions.quote: “judicial review” in the Anisminic era meant correctness review — that is, de novo consideration of the issue before the administrative tribunal which substituted the court’s perspective for that of the tribunal.

propositions.text: Crevier meant reasonable errors of law are not jurisdictional errors and can be shielded from correctness review.
propositions.quote: Crevier, following CUPE, meant that reasonable errors of law were not jurisdictional errors and could be shielded from correctness review.

propositions.text: Crevier did not intend privative clauses to shield unreasonable errors of fact or law from judicial correction.
propositions.quote: Crevier cannot have intended that unreasonable findings of fact or law could be shielded from judicial correction by a privative clause.

propositions.text: Unreasonable errors of fact and law are jurisdictional errors per established jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: unreasonable errors of fact and law are jurisdictional errors: see, e.g., Blanchard, at pp. 479-81, per Beetz J., and at pp. 493-95, per Lamer J.; see also Toronto (City) Board of Education, at paras. 44-46

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Crevier meant reasonable errors are shielded but unreasonable errors are jurisdictional and not shielded by privative clauses.

propositions.text: Nothing in Crevier departs from CUPE or the move from jurisdictional review to deference.
propositions.quote: Nothing in Crevier suggests that it is a departure from CUPE or out of step with the broader trend of this Court’s move from jurisdictional review to deference.

propositions.text: Privative clauses cannot preclude jurisdictional review per Chief Justice Laskin in Crevier.
propositions.quote: Chief Justice Laskin was explicit that privative clauses could not preclude jurisdictional review.

propositions.text: Privative clauses balance legislature's interests and courts' constitutional role but cannot limit jurisdictional issues.
propositions.quote: giving effect to privative clauses, particularly on questions of law, “balanced the competing interests of a provincial Legislature... and of the courts as ultimate interpreters... It cannot be left to a provincial statutory tribunal... to determine the limits of its own jurisdiction without appeal or review.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Crevier aligns with CUPE, affirming privative clauses cannot oust jurisdictional review, balancing legislature and courts' constitutional roles.

propositions.text: Since Crevier, s. 96 jurisprudence has liberalized to adapt to modern realities.
propositions.quote: our s. 96 jurisprudence has continued to undergo a “‘process of liberalization’ to adapt to modern realities”

propositions.text: Superior courts' existence and judicial review for legality are constitutionally guaranteed under s. 96.
propositions.quote: It is now well established that the existence of the superior courts is guaranteed by s. 96... and judicial review for legality... is entrenched by necessary implication in the core supervisory jurisdiction of those courts

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes s. 96 jurisprudence has liberalized, confirming superior courts' existence and judicial review for legality are constitutionally guaranteed.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review as defined in Vavilov is not constitutionally guaranteed minimum standard.
propositions.quote: I would not endorse that view. As products of our Court’s jurisprudence, the common law standards of review can be and have been modified over time.

propositions.text: Availability of legality review ensuring public power is within delegated authority is constitutionally guaranteed.
propositions.quote: What is clear is that the availability of legality review... is constitutionally guaranteed.

propositions.text: Vavilov's reasonableness review reflects broader rule of law and culture of justification considerations.
propositions.quote: broader considerations going to the rule of law and Canada’s constitutional “culture of justification” informed this Court’s restatement of reasonableness review in Vavilov

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Vavilov's reasonableness review is not constitutionally guaranteed, but legality review availability is guaranteed.

propositions.text: Irrational administrative decisions are unlawful as they exceed delegated authority limits.
propositions.quote: irrational administrative decisions are unlawful, insofar as they exceed the inherent limits of delegated authority.

propositions.text: Courts' power to protect against arbitrary public power lies at core of constitutionally protected jurisdiction under ss. 96 to 101.
propositions.quote: the power of the courts to protect against such arbitrariness lies... at the very heart of the courts’ constitutionally protected jurisdiction under ss. 96 to 101.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds irrational administrative decisions exceed delegated authority and courts' power to prevent arbitrariness is constitutionally protected.

propositions.text: Rationality review has constitutional aspect as boundary of legality.
propositions.quote: rationality review has a constitutional aspect. Rationality is a boundary of legality.

propositions.text: Deferential judicial review balances respect for legislature, executive, and courts as legality arbiters.
propositions.quote: deferential judicial review strikes the constitutionally necessary balance between respect for the democratic sovereignty of the legislature, respect for the competence and expertise of the executive, and respect for the courts as arbiters of legality

propositions.text: Judicial deference respects but does not submit to legislature and executive; courts remain essential for rule of law.
propositions.quote: Judicial deference to the legislature and the executive evinces respect without submission — the role of the courts remains essential, but the rule of law is not the rule of courts.

propositions.text: Courts' supervisory jurisdiction over legality does not preclude meaningful decision-making by other state actors.
propositions.quote: Provided that courts can exercise their supervisory jurisdiction over the legality of all exercises of public power, the rule of law does not preclude meaningful decision-making by other state actors

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds rationality review is constitutionally important, balancing respect for legislature, executive, and courts' legality role without submission.

propositions.text: Minimum constitutionally guaranteed standard of review is not before the Court and left for another day.
propositions.quote: the question of what minimum standard of review is constitutionally guaranteed is not before us, and should therefore be left to another day.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch's appeal does not require deciding when legislated standards offend rule of law limits.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch’s appeal does not require us to decide when a legislated standard of review will trench on the constitutional core of the courts’ supervisory jurisdiction and offend “the limits imposed by the rule of law”

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the minimum constitutional standard of review is not before it and will not be decided in this appeal.

propositions.text: Legislative limits on legality review are ultra vires because courts' role ensuring public power is sourced in law is constitutionally guaranteed.
propositions.quote: Legislative efforts to limit legality review are ultra vires not because reasonableness review, per se, is constitutionally entrenched, but because the Constitution guarantees the courts’ role in ensuring that all exercises of public power... are sourced in law.

propositions.text: Courts supervise delegated power exercises regardless of question type: fact, law, fairness, or other.
propositions.quote: Where an administrative decision-maker acts in an official capacity and exercises a delegated power, it does not matter whether that exercise of power concerns questions of fact, of law, of fairness, or any other issue

propositions.text: Judicial review guaranteed not only on questions of law but also other issues per Chief Justice Khullar's dissent in Northback Holdings.
propositions.quote: the notion advanced by some academic commentators that judicial review is guaranteed only on questions of law has no sound historical or jurisprudential basis

propositions.text: Courts are constitutionally empowered to supervise delegated power to ensure it respects inherent limits.
propositions.quote: What matters, for constitutional purposes, is that the courts are constitutionally empowered to supervise the exercise of delegated power to ensure it respects the boundaries of its inherent limits.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds legislative limits on legality review are ultra vires; courts' constitutional power to supervise delegated authority includes all question types.

propositions.text: Legislation ousting courts' constitutional power over judicial review is ultra vires and ineffective.
propositions.quote: Legislation that purports to oust this constitutional power of the courts oversteps the limits of the legislatures’ constitutional authority. Such efforts are ultra vires; they do not affect the scope of the courts’ supervisory jurisdiction.

propositions.text: This applies to s. 96 superior courts and Federal Courts with exclusive judicial review jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: This is true for the s. 96 superior courts, but also where the Federal Courts have been assigned exclusive jurisdiction over judicial review under the Federal Courts Act

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes legislation ousting courts' constitutional judicial review power is ultra vires, applying to s. 96 courts and Federal Courts alike.

propositions.text: Section 101 authorizes Parliament to transfer s. 96 courts' jurisdiction to other courts but cannot eliminate that jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Section 101 of the Constitution Act, 1867 authorizes Parliament to transfer some of the jurisdiction of the s. 96 courts... But the transfer cannot eliminate any portion of that jurisdiction

propositions.text: Parliament cannot limit judicial review to circumvent constitutional guarantee of legality when assigning jurisdiction to Federal Courts.
propositions.quote: Parliament cannot combine that allocation of jurisdiction with a limit on judicial review that would circumvent the constitutional guarantee of legality

propositions.text: Privative clauses preventing Federal Courts from exercising s. 96 supervisory jurisdiction are unconstitutional and void.
propositions.quote: A privative clause that prevents the Federal Courts from exercising a component of the s. 96 supervisory jurisdiction assigned to them is contrary to the Constitution Act, 1867 and of no force and effect.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s. 101 allows jurisdiction transfer but not elimination; privative clauses limiting Federal Courts' supervisory jurisdiction are unconstitutional.

propositions.text: Courts must consider substance of statutory provisions to determine if they oust judicial review for legality.
propositions.quote: courts must consider its substance: the question is whether, properly interpreted, the impugned provision has the effect of ousting judicial review for legality

paragraphs.summary: The Court states courts must assess whether a provision ousts judicial review for legality by considering its substance.

propositions.text: Legislatures may prescribe judicial review procedures without ousting courts' supervisory role.
propositions.quote: legislatures are competent to prescribe procedures for judicial review, provided that the supervisory role of the courts is not ousted.

propositions.text: Legislation may validly set timelines or fora for judicial review without foreclosing legality review.
propositions.quote: Legislation may, for example, validly set out specific timelines or fora for judicial review of certain issues without functionally foreclosing judicial review for legality.

propositions.text: Legislated standards of review are valid if respecting rule of law limits.
propositions.quote: legislated standards of review are valid, provided they respect the limits of the rule of law

propositions.text: Common law bases to decline judicial review (e.g., mootness) are consistent with rule of law and supervisory jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: the common law bases to decline to consider the merits of an application for judicial review... are fully consistent with the requirements of the rule of law: they constitute an exercise of, not a limit on, the supervisory jurisdiction of the courts.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains legislatures can set judicial review procedures and standards if courts' supervisory role remains intact and consistent with rule of law.

propositions.text: Legislation limiting courts' constitutionally enshrined supervisory jurisdiction is ultra vires.
propositions.quote: Where a statutory provision, properly construed, purports to limit any aspect of the courts’ constitutionally enshrined supervisory jurisdiction, that provision is ultra vires.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes any legislation limiting courts' constitutionally protected supervisory jurisdiction is ultra vires.

propositions.text: Section 66 of COIA states Commissioner's decisions are final and not reviewable except under Federal Courts Act grounds in s. 18.1(4)(a), (b), or (e).
propositions.quote: Every order and decision of the Commissioner is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s. 66 of COIA limits judicial review of Commissioner's decisions to specific grounds under the Federal Courts Act.

propositions.text: Section 66 limits judicial review to grounds in s. 18.1(4)(a), (b), and (e), excluding other grounds in s. 18.1(4).
propositions.quote: Section 66 is therefore explicit in limiting the scope of judicial review to the grounds set out in s. 18.1(4)(a), (b) and (e) of the Federal Courts Act. This excludes the following additional grounds that appear in the remainder of s. 18.1(4)

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 66 excludes some grounds for judicial review found in s. 18.1(4) of the Federal Courts Act.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch submits s. 18.1(4)(a) includes legality review on fact and law questions, so s. 66 does not bar such review.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch submits that the jurisdictional review referred to by s. 18.1(4)(a), understood in light of the history canvassed above, includes legality review on questions of fact and law. Since s. 66 permits review on the grounds included under s. 18.1(4)(a), Democracy Watch submits that its application for judicial review on questions of fact and law is not barred by s. 66.

propositions.text: Alternatively, if s. 66 bars review on fact and law, it is unconstitutional and should be invalidated.
propositions.quote: Alternatively, if s. 66 does bar judicial review on questions of fact and law, Democracy Watch submits that s. 66 is unconstitutional and should be declared of no force and effect.

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch argues s. 66 permits legality review on fact and law or is unconstitutional if it bars such review.

propositions.text: Courts have hesitated to say privative clauses cannot constitutionally achieve their intended effect, often reading them into constitutional compliance.
propositions.quote: While courts have often given little or no effect to privative clauses in their analysis, they have hesitated to say explicitly that such clauses cannot constitutionally accomplish what, on their face, they were intended to accomplish.

propositions.text: Dunsmuir's privative clause stated decisions are final and not reviewable, but Court held it indicates reasonableness review applies.
propositions.quote: The privative clause in Dunsmuir... stated explicitly that “every order... is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court”... the Dunsmuir Court held that the provision merely “gives rise to a strong indication that the reasonableness standard of review will apply”

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes courts often read privative clauses into constitutional compliance, as in Dunsmuir where a finality clause indicated reasonableness review.

propositions.text: Democracy Watch interprets s. 66 to allow jurisdictional review including questions of fact and law.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch’s proposed interpretation of s. 66 conforms to this tendency. Rather than state outright that s. 66 is ultra vires to the extent that it bars legality review on questions of fact and law, it invites this Court to read such questions into the ground of jurisdictional review permitted under s. 66.

paragraphs.summary: Democracy Watch argues s. 66 allows jurisdictional review including fact and law questions.

propositions.text: Parliament is presumed to respect constitutional constraints when enacting s. 66, but invalidity must be declared if no constitutional interpretation is possible.
propositions.quote: it is presumed that Parliament intended to respect its constitutional constraints: see R. v. Mills, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 668, at para. 56; R. v. J.J., 2022 SCC 28, [2022] 2 S.C.R. 3, at para. 18. The presumption of constitutionality is an important principle of statutory interpretation, but there are limits: where legislation is not amenable to a constitutionally compliant interpretation, the legislation must be declared invalid

paragraphs.summary: Court finds presumption of constitutionality applies but invalidity must be declared if no constitutional interpretation is possible.

propositions.text: Courts must not interpret privative clauses in ways fundamentally incompatible with legislative intent.
propositions.quote: Courts must not assign to these provisions meanings that are fundamentally incompatible with the intent of the enacting legislature.

paragraphs.summary: Court states courts must not interpret privative clauses incompatible with legislative intent.

propositions.text: Section 66 and s. 18.1(4) FCA do not permit legality review on questions of fact and law.
propositions.quote: Here, I cannot accept that s. 66, read together with s. 18.1(4) of the Federal Courts Act, permits legality review on questions of fact and law.

propositions.text: Section 66 separates review on fact and law from jurisdictional review, showing Parliament intended a narrow modern sense of jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: By expressly separating out review on questions of fact and law from review on jurisdictional grounds, s. 66 of the COIA suggests that Parliament’s intent was to invoke “jurisdiction” in its narrower, modern sense

propositions.text: Parliament clearly intended to exclude review on questions of fact and law in s. 66.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s clear intent in drafting s. 66 so as to expressly exclude review on questions of fact and law cannot be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 66 excludes legality review on fact and law questions, reflecting Parliament's clear intent.

propositions.text: Section 66 ousts judicial review on fact and law questions and is inconsistent with constitutional ss. 96-101, thus invalid under s. 52(1).
propositions.quote: To the extent it does so, s. 66 is inconsistent with ss. 96 to 101 of the Constitution Act, 1867 and, pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, should be declared of no force and effect.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes s. 66 ousts judicial review on fact and law and is constitutionally invalid.

propositions.text: All legal powers have inherent limits; no discretion is unfettered under the rule of law.
propositions.quote: All legal powers are subject to inherent limits. Under a constitutional order based in the rule of law, there is no such thing as an unfettered discretion

propositions.text: Courts ensure legal powers are exercised within limits; legislatures cannot shield delegated power from judicial review for legality.
propositions.quote: The courts are tasked with ensuring that legal powers are exercised in accordance with their limits: Vavilov, at para. 67. Parliament and the legislatures are not constitutionally competent to shield administrative exercises of delegated power from judicial review for legality on any ground

paragraphs.summary: Court states legal powers have limits; legislatures cannot shield delegated power from judicial review for legality.

propositions.text: Section 66's privative clause is invalid to the extent it bars judicial review on fact and law questions.
propositions.quote: The privative clause in s. 66 of the COIA should be declared of no force and effect to the extent that it purports to bar judicial review on questions of fact and law.

propositions.text: Section 66 does not prevent Democracy Watch's judicial review application.
propositions.quote: It poses no obstacle to Democracy Watch’s application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal erred in dismissing the application based on an adequate alternative to judicial review.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Federal Court of Appeal erred in dismissing the application on the basis that there is an adequate alternative to judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 66 invalid to bar judicial review, poses no obstacle to Democracy Watch, and Federal Court of Appeal erred.

propositions.text: Section 66 is invalid to bar judicial review on fact and law; appeal allowed with costs; matter remanded for Stage 2.
propositions.quote: I would declare that s. 66 of the COIA is of no force and effect to the extent it bars judicial review on questions of fact and law. I would allow Democracy Watch’s appeal with costs, set aside the order of the Federal Court of Appeal dismissing the application, and remand the matter to the court below to proceed to Stage 2. Appeal allowed with costs.

paragraphs.summary: Court declares s. 66 invalid to bar judicial review, allows appeal with costs, and remands for Stage 2.
